headline: LA's Urban Coyotes Are Increasingly at Home Above the Skyline
lede: On April 26, 2025, celebrity hair colorist Travis Ogletree glanced up through the glass skylight of his Hollywood Hills salon and found a coyote peering back — lapping pooled rainwater from the roof above. He posted the clip to TikTok with the caption "Just another day at the Treehouse." It went viral within hours, but the behavior it captured was, to anyone who tracks the species, entirely expected.
body:
Ogletree's Treehouse Studio sits in the Hollywood Hills, where commercial buildings are often carved into the hillside and rooflines can sit nearly flush with the slope behind them. That terrain, combined with coyotes' documented ability to jump up to eight feet and scale walls up to fourteen, makes a rooftop appearance less improbable than it looks. The **Santa Monica Mountains**, which begin just north of the neighborhood, form one of the most studied *urban wildlife corridors* — a mountain range bisected by freeways yet still home to mountain lions, deer, bobcats, and several hundred coyotes tracked by the National Park Service since 1996.

The NPS recently documented two GPS-collared coyotes in downtown Los Angeles: C-144, a female in the Westlake neighborhood who regularly crossed the 101 Freeway to raise five pups, and C-145, a male in Silver Lake whose GPS fixes fell in developed areas more than half the time and never in anything resembling natural habitat. Both were described as representing "some of the most urban *home ranges* of any coyote ever studied." A February 2025 paper in *Ecology Letters*, led by researchers at the California Academy of Sciences and UC Berkeley, found that human population density and development intensity were the strongest predictors of coyote movement across the city — surpassing vegetation cover and water availability. Lead author Dr. Christine Wilkinson observed that "urban areas are actually petri dishes where many social-ecological components come together in an acute way."

The incident arrived roughly three months after the January 2025 Palisades and Eaton fires burned through more than 37 square miles of the Santa Monica Mountains foothills and destroyed thousands of structures. Wildlife biologists warned that the fires pushed territorial animals — coyotes especially — into unfamiliar urban corridors, stripping away food and water. No reporting has confirmed that the Treehouse coyote was fire-displaced, but the timing coincides with documented heightened coyote activity in LA neighborhoods well outside the animals' usual habitat edges.

California's management approach has shifted sharply toward non-lethal tools: exclusion, deterrents, and public education rather than removal or relocation. Citizens for Los Angeles Wildlife states explicitly that removal "fails because it doesn't address underlying causes and may increase local populations through reduced territorial competition." The deeper concern is **habituation** — the gradual loss of wariness in animals repeatedly exposed to humans without consequence. A coyote confident enough to drink from a salon roof in daylight is well along that path. Ogletree's skylight provided a view that is becoming more available across the city, if usually without quite so good a punchline.

concepts.definition: A stretch of connected habitat — parks, hillsides, creek beds, or even freeway underpasses — that allows animals to move through an otherwise built-up environment. The Santa Monica Mountains function as the backbone of LA's corridor, linking the Simi Hills to the Pacific coast and funneling wildlife into surrounding neighborhoods.

The geographic area an animal regularly moves through in the course of its daily and seasonal activities — foraging, mating, denning. Unlike a defended territory, a home range may overlap with those of other individuals. Biologists track it via GPS collars to understand how animals use and adapt to their environment.

The process by which a wild animal gradually loses its instinctive fear of humans through repeated exposure without negative consequences. A habituated coyote may approach people, enter buildings, or appear in public spaces in daylight — increasing the likelihood of conflict and, ultimately, lethal removal.
